title: Beyond Oversquashing: Understanding Signal Propagation in GNNs Via Observables
claim: A signal can be decomposed into localized components, each described by an expected location and variance, which captures where signal mass lies.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, equation form with '=' and '+' operators
description: Three 1-D line plots are arranged left to right as an equation. The left panel shows a blue bimodal curve over x from -5 to 5. A shaded blue band spans roughly -1.6 to 2.1, and a blue dot near x=0.2 marks the expected location. A large '=' sign follows. The middle panel shows a red unimodal bump centered near x=-1.7, with a narrow pink band and a red dot at its mean. A '+' sign follows. The right panel shows a green unimodal bump centered near x=1.6, with a light green band and a green dot at its mean. Each panel has an x-axis with ticks at -4 to 4 and no y-axis. Color distinguishes the three signals. The eye goes first to the blue double-peaked curve, then to the red and green components that sum to it.
caption: Windowed localization of a graph signal. Decomposition of a signal $g$ to $g^0+g^1$. The horizontal axis is the real feature-location coordinate. Expected feature locations are marked by a dot, and the variance is signified by a color band.
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) perform computations on graphs by routing the signal between graph regions using a graph shift operator or a message passing scheme. Often, the propagation of the signal leads to a loss of information, where the signal tends to diffuse across the graph instead of being deliberately routed between regions of interest. Two notions that depict this phenomenon are oversmoothing and oversquashing. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach for modeling signal propagation, inspired by quantum mechanics, using the notion of observables. Specifically, we model the place in the graph where the signal lies, how much the signal is concentrated there, and how much of the signal is propagated towards a location of interest when applying a GNN. Using these new concepts, we prove that standard spectral GNNs have poor signal propagation capabilities. We then propose a new type of spectral GNN, termed SchrÃ¶dinger GNN, which we show has a superior capacity to route the signal across the graph.
